title: Reading practice: Fifteen Minutes to Read and a Class Message Board
description: Eight reading items about an argument for daily reading time and a class message board discussion, practicing finding claims, evidence and opposing views and responding to other writers.

stimuli.title: Fifteen Minutes to Read
paragraphs: Every day, middle school students move from class to class with packed schedules, and many of them rarely choose to read for pleasure. I believe that schools should set aside fifteen minutes each day for independent reading. This small change would help students become stronger readers and more thoughtful learners.

First, reading practice builds skills. Like athletes, readers improve through regular practice, and fifteen minutes a day adds up to more than an hour of reading each week. Students who read often meet more new words in context, which helps them understand difficult texts in every subject. For example, a student who reads about rivers in a novel may later recognize the same vocabulary in a science lesson.

Second, choice increases motivation. When students pick their own books, they are more likely to finish them. According to library records at the author’s school, checkouts doubled after teachers tried a trial reading period last spring.

Some teachers argue that the school day is already too short and that every minute should be spent on required lessons. This concern is reasonable. However, the reading period would take only a small part of the day, and the skills students gain would help them learn the required material more effectively. Therefore, the benefits outweigh the cost.
A school that values reading should give students time to do it. Fifteen minutes is a modest request, but it could change how students think about books.

stimuli.title: Class Message Board: Should the Science Fair Be Moved?
paragraphs: Posted by Priya: Our science fair is scheduled for Friday, but the school choir concert is on Thursday evening, and six students in our class are singing in it. I think we should move the science fair to the following Tuesday. If the fair stays on Friday, the choir members will be tired and may not have enough time to finish their projects. Also, moving it would give everyone four more days to practice their presentations.
Posted by Mr. Alvarez (teacher): Thank you for the suggestion, Priya. Please remember that the gym is available only on Friday this week, and the judges have already agreed to come on that day.

Posted by Diego: I disagree with Priya. A Tuesday date would be a problem because the judges cannot come, and we cannot hold the fair without them. However, we could let the choir members present first on Friday so they can go home early. That way, no one has to give up the fair.
Posted by Priya: Diego’s idea solves the problem of the judges. I agree to keep Friday if the choir members can present first.

items.stem: Which TWO details support the author’s reason that daily reading builds skills?

options.text: Library checkouts doubled after a trial reading period last spring.
Students who read often meet more new words in context as they read.
Some teachers say that the school day is already too short for extra work.
Fifteen minutes a day adds up to more than an hour of reading each week.

distractors.a: This detail supports the author’s point about choice and motivation, not about building skills.
distractors.c: This is the opposing view, not a reason that supports daily reading.

items.explanation: The second paragraph explains that practice builds skills: reading often means meeting more new words in context, and fifteen minutes a day adds up to more than an hour each week.

support.clue: Look at the second paragraph, which begins with “First.” Choose details that explain how reading practice improves reading ability.
support.frame: Daily reading builds skills because ______ and because ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different skill). “Drawing every day builds skill. A beginner who sketches for ten minutes a day gets more practice, and she notices details in shapes more easily.” Two details explain how practice improves the skill. Find two details like these in the second paragraph.

misconceptions.a: picks evidence for a different reason
misconceptions.c: confuses an opposing view with support

facts: Fifteen minutes a day for five school days is 75 minutes, which is more than an hour.

items.stem: Choose the phrases that best complete a summary of the text.

dropdown.template: The author argues that schools should {1}. The first reason is that reading often {2}. The second reason is that students {3}.

options: give students fifteen minutes of reading homework each night
set aside fifteen minutes each day for independent reading
end the school day fifteen minutes earlier for free time
1.answer: set aside fifteen minutes each day for independent reading

options: gives students more practice with new words in context
helps students skip the required lessons in other subjects
makes it easier for students to find books in the library
2.answer: gives students more practice with new words in context

options: prefer short books that take less time to finish
do better when teachers choose every book for them
are more likely to finish books they choose themselves
3.answer: are more likely to finish books they choose themselves

items.explanation: The first paragraph states the claim, the paragraph beginning “First” gives the skills reason, and the paragraph beginning “Second” gives the choice reason.

support.clue: Skim the first paragraph for the author’s claim. Then find the paragraphs that begin with “First” and “Second.”
support.frame: The author’s claim is that schools should ______. First, ______. Second, ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different argument). “Cities should plant more trees. First, trees give shade on hot days. Second, trees make streets look welcoming.” A summary names the claim and then each reason in order. Build your summary of the reading text the same way.

items.stem: Sort each statement from the text: is it the author’s claim, support for the claim, or the opposing view?

tokens.text: Schools should set aside fifteen minutes each day for independent reading.
Library records show that checkouts doubled after a trial reading period.
The school day is already too short for extra activities.
Students are more likely to finish books that they choose themselves.
Every minute should be spent on required lessons.

items.explanation: The author’s claim is stated in the first paragraph. The checkout records and the point about choice support it. The teachers’ concerns about a short school day are the opposing view.

support.clue: Ask who would say each sentence: the author, or the teachers who disagree? Then decide whether an author’s sentence is the main claim or a reason that supports it.
support.model: Mentor example (a different argument). Claim: “Our school should have a recycling team.” Support: “Last year, recycling cut our trash by a third.” Opposing view: “Some students say they are too busy to join.” Sort the reading text’s sentences into the same three groups.

facts: The school and its library records described in the text are fictional.

items.stem: How does the author respond to the concern that the school day is already too short?

options.text: The author rejects the concern and promises that the school would lose no time at all.
The author calls the concern reasonable, but says the benefits are greater than the cost.
The author accepts the concern and changes the claim to reading at home instead.
The author agrees with the concern and decides to end the argument there.

distractors.a: The author calls the concern reasonable and says the period would take a small part of the day. The text does not say that no time would be lost.
distractors.c: The author’s claim stays the same: the reading period would happen at school.
distractors.d: The author continues with “However” and “Therefore” and still argues for the reading period.

items.explanation: The author says the concern is reasonable, uses “However” to point out that the period is small, and concludes with “Therefore” that the benefits outweigh the cost.

support.clue: Find the paragraph that begins “Some teachers argue.” Read its last three sentences and ask what the author does after naming the concern.
support.frame: The author says the concern is ______, and then ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different response). A writer notes that some students dislike homework. She writes, “That is true for long assignments, but short practice helps memory, so it is worth the time.” She first accepts a point and then gives a stronger point. Look for the same two moves in the paragraph about the teachers’ concern.

misconceptions.a: ignores the admission that the concern is reasonable
misconceptions.c: assumes the author changes the claim
misconceptions.d: assumes the author gives up the argument

items.stem: Put the parts of the text in the order that the author presents them.

items.text: The author answers the concern that the school day is too short.
The author explains that regular reading practice builds skills.
The author ends by saying that a school that values reading should give students time to read.
The author states the claim that schools should set aside daily reading time.
The author explains that choosing books increases motivation.

items.explanation: The text moves from the claim to the first reason, the second reason, the answer to the opposing concern, and a closing statement.

support.clue: Read the first sentence of each paragraph and ask what the writer is doing in it.
support.frame: The first paragraph ______. The middle paragraphs ______. Near the end, the writer ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different text). A short essay about a town pet shelter opens with a story about a lost dog, then states the claim, and then gives reasons. Writers do not always use the same order, so look at what each paragraph does. Check what each paragraph in the reading text does.

items.stem: Choose the connecting words that best explain the plan on the message board.

dropdown.template: The science fair will probably stay on Friday {1} the gym is available only that day and the judges have already agreed to come. Priya suggested a new date {2} six classmates were singing in a concert the night before. Diego’s plan lets the choir members present first, {3} no one has to give up the fair.

items.explanation: “Because” gives the reason the fair will probably stay on Friday, “since” gives Priya’s reason for suggesting a new date, and “so that” gives the purpose of Diego’s plan.

support.clue: Decide for each blank whether the second idea gives a reason or a purpose. Reread Mr. Alvarez’s post and Diego’s post.
support.frame: The fair will probably stay on Friday ______ the gym and the judges are available only that day. Diego’s plan lets the choir present first ______ no one gives up the fair.
support.model: Mentor example (a different decision). “The trip stayed on Monday, as the bus was booked only that day. Mina suggested an early lunch in order to finish before the rain.” The first connecting word gives a reason, and the second shows a purpose. Choose the connecting words that fit the message board.

items.stem: Match each post to what the writer does in it.

right.text: States a request and gives reasons
Explains why the request cannot be done as asked

items.explanation: Priya asks for a new date and gives reasons, Mr. Alvarez explains the gym and judge limits, Diego disagrees and offers a compromise, and Priya agrees to it.

support.clue: Read the first sentences of each post. Ask whether the writer is asking, explaining, disagreeing, or agreeing.
support.frame: In this post, the writer ______ by saying ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different thread). Post 1: “Can we have lunch outside? It’s sunny, and indoors is crowded.” Post 2: “We can’t, because the field is closed today.” Post 1 makes a request with reasons, and Post 2 explains why not. Name what each post in your thread does.

facts: The message board scenario is fictional.

items.stem: Sort each sentence from the message board: does the writer disagree or agree?

tokens.text: Diego’s idea solves the problem of the judges.
A Tuesday date would be a problem because the judges cannot come.
I agree to keep Friday if the choir members can present first.

items.explanation: “I disagree” and “would be a problem” show disagreement, while “solves the problem” and “I agree” show agreement.

support.clue: Look at the signal words and phrases in each sentence. Ask whether the writer is accepting the earlier post or arguing against it.
support.frame: This writer ______ because the sentence says ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different thread). “I disagree with moving the picnic, because the park is booked” shows disagreement. “Your plan fixes the problem” shows agreement. Signal words show which side a writer is on. Look for signal words in the message board.

facts: The message board scenario is fictional.
